Milliman 1982.title: Using Background Music to Affect the Behavior of Supermarket Shoppers
Milliman 1982.summary: Slow music → 38% higher daily sales (but didn't replicate at scale)
Milliman 1982.killer_stat: 38.2% higher daily sales — a $4,627/day difference — from nothing more than slowing down the background music. That's roughly $1.7 million in annualized revenue for a single store.
Milliman 1982.story: In 1980, Ronald Milliman convinced a medium-sized supermarket in a southwestern U.S. city to let him secretly run an experiment on its shoppers for nine weeks. He piped in three different audio conditions on different days — no music, slow-tempo instrumental music (averaging 60 BPM), and fast-tempo instrumental music (averaging 108 BPM) — and measured two things: how fast people moved through the aisles, and how much money the store made each day.

Milliman 1986.title: The Influence of Background Music on the Behavior of Restaurant Patrons
Milliman 1986.citation: Milliman, R.E. (1986). Journal of Consumer Research, 13(2), 286–289.
Milliman 1986.summary: Slow music → 11 min longer stay → 3 more drinks per table
Milliman 1986.killer_stat: 3.04 additional drinks per table with slow music — roughly a 40% increase in beverage revenue. And an 11-minute longer stay (56 vs 45 minutes).
Milliman 1986.story: Four years after his supermarket breakthrough, Milliman ran the same slow-vs-fast tempo experiment in a restaurant in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Same BPM cutoffs (≤72 slow, ≥94 fast). But the restaurant context revealed a much richer story than the grocery store.

North 1999.title: The Influence of In-Store Music on Wine Selections
North 1999.citation: North, A.C., Hargreaves, D.J., & McKendrick, J. (1999). Journal of Applied Psychology, 84(2), 271–276. Also published as a brief in Nature, 390, 132 (1997).
North 1999.summary: French music → 5:1 French wine. German music reversed it. Nobody noticed.
North 1999.killer_stat: 5:1 French wine preference with French music. 2:1 German wine preference with German music. And only 14% of shoppers (6 out of 44) realized the music had influenced them.
North 1999.story: This is the most famous study in retail music research, and the one that makes every audience sit up.

Areni 1993.title: The Influence of Background Music on Shopping Behavior: Classical Versus Top-Forty Music in a Wine Store
Areni 1993.citation: Areni, C.S. & Kim, D. (1993). Advances in Consumer Research, 20, 336–340.
Areni 1993.summary: Classical music → more expensive wines selected (not more bottles)
Areni 1993.killer_stat: Significant shift to higher price tiers — same number of bottles purchased, but more expensive selections. The effect was purely on price-per-item, not on volume.
Areni 1993.story: Over two months of Friday and Saturday evenings, researchers alternated between classical music and Top-40 hits in a wine store. They wanted to know: does the genre of background music affect what people buy?

Smith 1966.title: Arousal Hypothesis and the Effects of Music on Purchasing Behavior
Smith 1966.citation: Smith, P.C. & Curnow, R. (1966). Journal of Applied Psychology, 50(3), 255–256.
Smith 1966.summary: Loud = faster exit, but same total sales. Volume controls velocity.
Smith 1966.killer_stat: 1,100 shoppers observed. Loud music = significantly less time in store. But no change in total sales. People speed up, they don't buy less.
Smith 1966.story: This is the earliest empirical study of music and shopping behavior — published in 1966, when the Beatles were still together. Smith and Curnow tested a brutally simple question in two supermarkets: does loud music make people leave faster?

Donovan 1982.title: Store Atmosphere: An Environmental Psychology Approach
Donovan 1982.citation: Donovan, R.J. & Rossiter, J.R. (1982). Journal of Retailing, 58(Spring), 34–57.
Donovan 1982.summary: Pleasure predicts everything. The theoretical foundation.
Donovan 1982.killer_stat: Of the three PAD dimensions, only Pleasure was a significant and consistent predictor of approach behavior (intended time, spending, and return visits). Arousal and Dominance were not.
Donovan 1982.story: Before this paper, retailers thought about store atmosphere the way you'd think about wallpaper — nice to have, hard to quantify. Donovan and Rossiter changed that by importing the Mehrabian-Russell environmental psychology model into retail for the first time.

Donovan 1994.title: Store Atmosphere and Purchasing Behavior
Donovan 1994.citation: Donovan, R.J., Rossiter, J.R., Marcoolyn, G., & Nesdale, A. (1994). Journal of Retailing, 70(3), 283–294.
Donovan 1994.summary: Pleasure at 5 minutes → predicts real unplanned spending
Donovan 1994.killer_stat: Pleasure measured at the 5-minute mark predicted actual incremental spending — the gap between what shoppers planned to spend and what they actually spent.
Donovan 1994.story: The 1982 study had a fatal flaw: it only measured what people *said* they'd do, using college students. Twelve years later, Donovan came back with the real test: actual shoppers, actual money, measured in the wild.

Yalch 2000.title: The Effects of Music in a Retail Setting on Real and Perceived Shopping Times
Yalch 2000.citation: Yalch, R.F. & Spangenberg, E.R. (2000). Journal of Business Research, 49(2), 139–147.
Yalch 2000.summary: Unfamiliar music = more actual time, less perceived time. Inverted.
Yalch 2000.killer_stat: Actual time: longer with unfamiliar music. Perceived time: longer with familiar music. The two were inverted. Unfamiliar music extends dwell while compressing time perception — the ideal combination.
Yalch 2000.story: This study uncovered one of the most counterintuitive findings in the field — a genuine paradox that most people get backwards.

Knoferle 2012.title: It Is All in the Mix
Knoferle 2012.citation: Knoferle, K.M. et al. (2012). Marketing Letters, 23(1), 325–337.
Knoferle 2012.summary: Slow+minor = best. Major key eliminates the tempo effect entirely.
Knoferle 2012.killer_stat: ~12% higher sales for slow+minor vs. fast+minor. Major mode eliminated the tempo effect entirely — slow-major ≈ fast-major.
Knoferle 2012.story: For 30 years after Milliman, everyone focused on tempo. Slow = more dwell = more sales. Simple. But Knoferle and colleagues suspected something was being missed: the *mode* of the music (major key vs. minor key).

Knoferle 2017.title: An Upbeat Crowd: Fast In-store Music Alleviates Negative Effects of High Social Density on Customers' Spending
Knoferle 2017.citation: Knoferle, K.M., Paus, V.C., & Vossen, A. (2017). Journal of Retailing, 93(4), 541–549.
Knoferle 2017.summary: Fast music helps when crowded (43,676 observations). Slow doesn't.
Knoferle 2017.killer_stat: 43,676 basket observations. Fast music during crowding → ~8% higher basket value vs. no music. Driven by more items (not more expensive items).
Knoferle 2017.story: This study overturns the "slow is always better" dogma with the most robust dataset in the field: 43,676 shopping basket observations from six European grocery convenience stores over a six-week experiment.

Mattila 2001.title: Congruency of Scent and Music as a Driver of In-Store Evaluations and Behavior
Mattila 2001.citation: Mattila, A.S. & Wirtz, J. (2001). Journal of Retailing, 77(2), 273–289.
Mattila 2001.summary: Scent+music must match on arousal. Mismatch is worse than either alone.
Mattila 2001.killer_stat: 270 customers in a real gift shop. Congruent arousal conditions → significantly higher approach behavior, impulse purchases, AND satisfaction. Incongruent → worse than either stimulus alone.
Mattila 2001.story: Mattila and Wirtz asked a question most music-only researchers had ignored: what happens when you combine music with scent? Is 1+1=2, or does it depend on whether they match?

Sherman 1997.title: Store Environment and Consumer Purchase Behavior: Mediating Role of Consumer Emotions
Sherman 1997.citation: Sherman, E., Mathur, A., & Smith, R.B. (1997). Psychology & Marketing, 14(4), 361–378.
Sherman 1997.summary: Environment → emotion → behavior. Impulse buying is emotional, not cognitive.
Sherman 1997.killer_stat: Both pleasure (→ money spent, store affinity) and arousal (→ money, time, number of items) were significant mediators between store environment and actual purchase behavior.
Sherman 1997.story: Sherman and colleagues ran a large-scale field study to answer a fundamental question: do store environments affect actual purchase behavior through emotions, or through rational evaluation?

Andersson 2012.title: Let the Music Play or Not
Andersson 2012.citation: Andersson, P.K. et al. (2012). Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services, 19(6), 553–560.
Andersson 2012.summary: Any music > silence. +8 min dwell, more spending. Table stakes.
Andersson 2012.killer_stat: 8 additional minutes of dwell time with music vs. silence, leading to significantly increased spending. N=550 across two retail contexts.
Andersson 2012.story: Before you can argue about tempo, mode, or genre, you need to answer a more basic question: does having music at all make a difference compared to silence?

Biswas 2019.title: Sounds Like a Healthy Retail Atmospheric Strategy
Biswas 2019.citation: Biswas, D., Lund, K., & Szocs, C. (2019). Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 47(1), 37–55.
Biswas 2019.summary: Low volume → healthier food choices. High volume → junk food.
Biswas 2019.killer_stat: 20% more patrons ordered unhealthy food when music was loud (70 dB) vs. quiet (55 dB). 549 items tracked across field experiment days.
Biswas 2019.story: Most music research asks "does this sell more?" Biswas and colleagues asked something different: does music volume affect *what* people choose to buy?

Beverland 2006.title: In-Store Music and Consumer–Brand Relationships
Beverland 2006.citation: Beverland, M.B. et al. (2006). Journal of Business Research, 59(9), 982–989.
Beverland 2006.summary: Music fit strengthens brand. Misfit actively damages it.
Beverland 2006.killer_stat: No quantitative stat — but the qualitative finding is clear: misfit music actively damages brand perception. It's not a neutral miss; it's a negative event.
Beverland 2006.story: This is a qualitative study, which means no statistical effect sizes — but it tells a story that quantitative studies can't. The researchers did in-depth interviews with 20 consumers plus observational research in themed retail stores across Australia and the US, asking: what happens to your relationship with a brand when the music *fits* versus when it *doesn't*?

Spangenberg 2005.title: It's Beginning to Smell (and Sound) a Lot Like Christmas
Spangenberg 2005.citation: Spangenberg, E.R., Grohmann, B., & Sprott, D.E. (2005). Journal of Business Research, 58(11), 1583–1589.
Spangenberg 2005.summary: Pine scent alone backfired. Needed Christmas music to work.
Spangenberg 2005.killer_stat: Congruent (Christmas music + pine scent) → significantly higher store attitudes, visit intentions, and pleasure than all other conditions. Pine scent alone → negative effect.
Spangenberg 2005.story: The title alone makes this memorable. Spangenberg used the Christmas season as a natural laboratory for multisensory congruence. In a simulated retail store, 140 undergraduate students experienced four conditions: Christmas music + pine scent (congruent), Christmas music alone, pine scent alone, or neither.

Sun 2023.title: The Effects of Background Music Tempo on Consumer Variety-Seeking Behavior
Sun 2023.citation: Sun, W., Chang, E.-C., & Xu, Y. (2023). Frontiers in Psychology, 14, 1236006. (Open access)
Sun 2023.summary: Fast tempo → more variety seeking. Arousal mediates. Lab-only.
Sun 2023.killer_stat: 5 experiments consistently showing fast tempo → increased variety-seeking. Arousal is the confirmed mediator.
Sun 2023.story: This is one of the few studies connecting music to *what* people buy rather than *how much*. Across five lab experiments at Renmin University of China, the researchers showed that fast-tempo background music increases variety-seeking behavior — when given a choice of snack flavors, people exposed to fast music chose a wider variety.

Lammers 2003.title: An Oceanside Field Experiment on Background Music Effects on the Restaurant Tab
Lammers 2003.citation: Lammers, H.B. (2003). Perceptual and Motor Skills, 96(3), 1025–1026.
Lammers 2003.summary: Soft music → $3.05 more per check. Genre didn't matter.
Lammers 2003.killer_stat: $3.05 per check more with soft vs. loud music (~15% lift). Genre made zero difference.
Lammers 2003.story: Sometimes the simplest studies tell the clearest story. At an oceanside restaurant in California, Lammers crossed two music variables — volume (soft vs. loud) and genre (soft rock vs. classical) — and tracked restaurant checks.

Caldwell 1999.title: Play That One Again: The Effect of Music Tempo on Consumer Behaviour in a Restaurant
Caldwell 1999.citation: Caldwell, C. & Hibbert, S.A. (1999). European Advances in Consumer Research, 4, 58–62.
Caldwell 1999.summary: Slow jazz → 15 min longer. But spending didn't proportionally follow.
Caldwell 1999.killer_stat: 15 minutes longer dining duration with slow vs. fast tempo jazz. But spending gains did not proportionally match the time extension.
Caldwell 1999.story: Caldwell and Hibbert extended Milliman's restaurant work with a tighter design: all jazz music from a single artist (controlling for genre effects), same BPM cutoffs (≤72 slow, ≥94 fast), in a real restaurant. Data was collected from two specific tables on Thursdays and Sundays.

Alpert 1990.title: Music Influences on Mood and Purchase Intentions
Alpert 1990.citation: Alpert, J.I. & Alpert, M.I. (1990). Psychology & Marketing, 7(2), 109–133.
Alpert 1990.summary: Sad music > happy for greeting cards. Emotional congruence > simple positivity.
Alpert 1990.killer_stat: Sad music > happy music for purchase intention. Music influenced buying intent without affecting intervening cognitions — it bypassed rational processing.
Alpert 1990.story: Alpert and Alpert set up one of the earliest controlled experiments on musical emotion and purchasing. Students were exposed to greeting card advertisements accompanied by happy instrumental music, sad instrumental music, or silence. The music was carefully selected — equally liked but unfamiliar, matched on structural analysis.

Grossman 2025.title: The Impact of Background Music Style on Price Thresholds
Grossman 2025.citation: Grossman, O. & Rachamim, M. (2025). Marketing Letters. DOI: 10.1007/s11002-025-09803-4
Grossman 2025.summary: Classical raises max WTP — but only for hedonic products + high pleasure.
Grossman 2025.killer_stat: Classical music raises maximum acceptable price for hedonic products when pleasure is high. No effect on minimum price, no effect on utilitarian products, no effect when pleasure is low.
Grossman 2025.story: This study adds precision to the Areni & Kim finding about classical music and pricing. Grossman and Rachamim (Bar-Ilan University, Israel) measured not just "did they spend more?" but specifically: did the music change the *minimum* acceptable price, the *maximum* acceptable price, or both?

EMAC 2025.title: Background Music in Retail: When Taking It Slow May Benefit You
EMAC 2025.citation: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (2025). EMAC 2025 Conference Proceedings. Part of EU project Music360. URL: https://proceedings.emac-online.org/pdfs/A2025-126256.pdf
EMAC 2025.summary: No overall tempo effect at scale. Only loyalty members responded.
EMAC 2025.killer_stat: 140 stores. No overall tempo effect on sales. Slow music only boosted spending among loyalty program members. Fast music → higher employee satisfaction.
EMAC 2025.story: This is the study that humbles everyone who cites Milliman. In spring 2024, researchers from Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam partnered with a large Dutch national retailer, Dutch music rights organizations (BUMA and SENA), and music tech company BMAT to run the largest field experiment on music tempo ever conducted: 140 stores, 6 weeks, real sales data.

Zwebner 2014.title: The Temperature Premium: Warm Temperatures Increase Product Valuation
Zwebner 2014.citation: Zwebner, Y., Lee, L., & Goldenberg, J. (2014). Journal of Consumer Psychology, 24(2), 251–259.
Zwebner 2014.summary: Warm temps → 10-36% higher WTP. Not music, but a critical covariate.
Zwebner 2014.killer_stat: 36% higher WTP from holding a warm pad for just 10 seconds. 10.4% overall temperature premium across studies.
Zwebner 2014.story: This isn't a music study — and that's exactly why it's in this collection. Zwebner and colleagues (including Leonard Lee from Columbia Business School) ran five studies showing that physical warmth increases how much people will pay for products.

Margulis 2014.title: On Repeat: How Music Plays the Mind
Margulis 2014.citation: Margulis, E.H. (2014). On Repeat: How Music Plays the Mind. Oxford University Press. Winner of the Wallace Berry Award (Society for Music Theory) and ASCAP Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award.
Margulis 2014.summary: Repetition → absorption → time distortion. 94% of music repeats. Zero retail evidence.
Margulis 2014.killer_stat: 94% of musical passages are literally repeated at some point across cultures. And adding repetition to unfamiliar music made listeners rate it as more enjoyable, higher quality, and more human.
Margulis 2014.story: This is a book, not a single study — and it's the theoretical backbone for why musical repetition affects time perception and immersive states.

Herrington 1996.title: Effects of Music in Service Environments: A Field Study
Herrington 1996.citation: Herrington, J.D. & Capella, L.M. (1996). The Journal of Services Marketing, 10(2), 26–41.
Herrington 1996.summary: Preference was the ONLY significant predictor. Tempo/volume → not significant.
Herrington 1996.killer_stat: Musical preference was the only significant predictor of shopping time and spending. Tempo and volume effects → not significant.
Herrington 1996.story: This study is the cold water on the tidy tempo-and-volume narrative. In a supermarket field study, Herrington and Capella tested three music variables simultaneously: tempo, volume, and personal musical preference. They measured shopping time and spending.

Broekemier 2008.title: An Exploration of Happy/Sad and Liked/Disliked Music Effects on Shopping Intentions
Broekemier 2008.citation: Broekemier, G., Marquardt, R., & Gentry, J.W. (2008). Journal of Services Marketing, 22(1), 59–67.
Broekemier 2008.summary: Happy+liked = best. Sad+disliked = worst. Likeability is the constraint.
Broekemier 2008.killer_stat: Happy + liked = highest shopping intentions. Sad + disliked = lowest. The interaction matters more than either dimension alone.
Broekemier 2008.story: Broekemier and colleagues set up the definitive comparison: which matters more for shopping intentions — whether the music is *happy or sad* (emotional valence, which a system can control) or whether the shopper *likes or dislikes* it (personal preference, which a system can't fully control)?

North 2003.title: The Effect of Musical Style on Restaurant Customers' Spending
North 2003.citation: North, A.C., Shilcock, A., & Hargreaves, D.J. (2003). Environment and Behavior, 35(5), 712–718.
North 2003.killer_stat: £32.52 per head with classical music vs. £29.46 with pop and £29.73 with no music. Classical produced ~10% higher spending. Pop ≈ silence.
North 2003.story: Adrian North — the same researcher who ran the famous wine aisle priming study — tested classical vs. pop vs. no music across 18 evenings in a British restaurant. Six evenings per condition. He tracked mean spend per head across every line item: starters, mains, desserts, coffee, bar, wine, total food, total drink, and total spend.

Doucé 2020.title: Sensory Overload in a Shopping Environment
Doucé 2020.citation: Doucé, L. & Adams, C. (2020). Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services, 57, 102154.
Doucé 2020.summary: Third high-arousal stimulus from a "higher sense" → overload → avoidance
Doucé 2020.killer_stat: Sensory overload = third high-arousal stimulus from a "higher sense." Result: arousal up + pleasure down → avoidance.
Doucé 2020.story: Every other study in this collection says "add this stimulus, improve this outcome." Doucé and Adams asked the opposite question: when does adding *too many* stimuli backfire?
